children: New Delhi, Oct. 18 -- Yes Bank would have reported a net loss of Rs.5,217 crore in the September quarter had it recognised the impact of the Supreme Court verdict overturning the write-off of its additional tier-1 (AT-1) bonds worth Rs.8,415 crore, the bank said in its Q2 investor presentation filed with the stock exchanges.
The private-sector lender, 24.9% owned by Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, reported a net profit of Rs.1,080 crore for the July-September, according to earnings announced on Saturday.

Had the judgement's impact been known, its CET-1 capital ratio would have dropped to 11.4% from the reported 13.7%, while its return on assets would have turned negative at 4.3%, compared with the reported positive 0.9%.

The lender noted that these pro forma estimates, including the estimated loss, are subject to revision based on the consequential actions, further legal assessment and final accounting and regulatory treatment.

"Pending completion of this assessment and determination of the appropriate accounting treatment, no impact arising from the judgment has been recognised in the reported Q2FY27 financial results," the bank said.
Yes Bank's net profit rose 65% year-on-year to Rs.1,080 crore in the September quarter, while remaining largely flat sequentially.

Operating profit rose 29.4% to Rs.1,678 crore, and net interest income rose 22.7% to Rs.2,822 crore. Asset quality also improved, with gross non-performing assets (NPAs) declining to 1.2% from 1.6% a year earlier.

The bank said it is evaluating options to strengthen its capital buffers to support future growth. It added that it respects the Supreme Court's judgment and is assessing the consequential actions, implementation requirements, financial and regulatory implications, and available legal remedies.

Yes Bank sank into a liquidity crisis in March 2020 as bad loans swelled, prompting the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to take control of the lender and freeze withdrawals. A consortium of lenders led by the State Bank of India (SBI) was assembled to bail out the bank by injecting fresh equity capital.
As part of the rescue exercise, the bank's administrator wrote off around Rs.8,415 crore worth of AT-1 bonds, prompting Axis Trustee Services and other bondholders to move court.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court dismissed appeals challenging the Bombay High Court's order that quashed the write-off earlier.

"The question is not whether the AT-1 bonds could have been or ought to have been written down off. The question is the manner in which it was done," the judgment penned by justices Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih said.

The administrator could not exercise a power reserved for the RBI, the court said, noting the write-down was contrary to the RBI's own master circular on Basel-III capital regulations and the terms governing the bonds.

Yes Bank shares plunged 14.5% to Rs.18.12 on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) after the judgement was passed, turning the worst-performer in the Nifty Bank index as investors fretted about the ruling's financial impact.

AT-1 bonds do not have a fixed maturity date, meaning banks are not required to repay the principal on a predetermined date but must make coupon payments subject to the bonds' terms and applicable regulations.
Most such bonds also carry a call option, typically exercisable after five or 10 years, allowing the bank to redeem them early.

Therefore, unless the verdict is overturned, Yes Bank will have to restart making yearly coupon payments to bondholders, Mint reported earlier. However, the fate of the past dues, from 2020 to now, could not be immediately ascertained.
